**Dossier 1:** Criminalisation of trans expression (Article 521, up to 6 years), morality provisions, arrests, anal examinations, ban on LGBT gatherings, documented rise in prejudice/violence in capital, no LGR, no border/facility info. Also some judicial progress (2023 ruling on consensual relations, court froze gathering ban, 2015 marker change). This is a state that criminalises trans expression with enforcement documented. Severity: imprisonment. Not execution. Tier 1-2: criminalisation of expression is a state-imposed exposure. Score maybe 0.20-0.28. Given arrests documented, prosecutions, anal exams, activist crackdown, rising violence — but also courts pushing back. The direct trans-specific criminal statute (Article 521) with explicit criminalisation of trans feminine presentation, plus police arrests. I'd say ~0.20-0.25. Let's say 0.22.

**Dossier 2:** Strong protections: hate speech law covering trans, anti-discrimination, hate crime framework, self-ID LGR (climate), generally liberal society. Negatives: rising hate crimes, 2022 Pride mass shooting (severe but isolated, sentenced to max), 8% reporting, clearance rate drop, far-right/anti-trans groups, 11% hostile attitudes. Border/facility not addressed. This is well above reduced risk. Comparable to calibration 0.75 or 0.85. Mass shooting is a serious incident but one-off; documented hate crime rise with falling clearance. Society generally liberal, protections exist and operate (30-year sentence). I'd say 0.78-0.82. Let's say 0.80.

**Dossier 3:** No criminalisation of trans, same-sex legal. No anti-discrimination law, no hate crime recognition, LGR requires surgery (resident), marriage banned, strong social hostility (78% opposed same-sex marriage in 2017, 12% approval 2023), dominant religious institution opposed. One indigenous territory with accepted third gender. No documented police targeting, no border issues documented. No universal exposure documented. So: societal hostility tier 3, thin recourse (no hate crime law, no AD law). But no documented visitor-facing restriction. Social conservatism with documented majority hostility toward gender/sexual diversity. Hmm. No criminalisation of trans expression. Absence of AD law is resident gap mostly. Social hostility: 12% approval of same-sex marriage, religious institution leading opposition — that's social hostility (b) framing moral offender. I'd place around 0.50-0.58. Given strong documented social disapproval but no trans-specific legal exposure and one documented acceptance pocket... Dossier 3 lacks documented working protections and has strong hostility signals. ~0.52.

**Dossier 4:** Very strong protections: marriage equality, no-surgery LGR, criminalised transphobia, hate crime framework, X marker on passports/IDs, custody placement by preference with LGBTI units, free SRS, courts awarding damages against discriminatory businesses, domestic violence law extended to trans women. Negatives: significant violence/discrimination in practice (2026 review), one state prison system housing trans women in masculine units (residents), minors' care ban litigation, drink-spiking robberies in one city, death threats to gay representative. Custody resolution is positive and national — but practice diverges in one state (residents). Traveller facing: X markers accepted, no facility restrictions documented, official guidance affirms bathroom rights. Strong. Comparable to 0.85 anchor. Maybe 0.85-0.88. Violence documented ("significant violence") — but protections operate. I'd say 0.85.

**Dossier 5:** Criminalises same-sex conduct (life imprisonment for buggery) but prosecutions rare; cross-dressing offence struck down 2018; no LGR; police use residual clauses to extort LGBT people (documented); a trans woman stabbed, then refused court entry and case dismissed (state failure); 69 documented violence cases 2018-2022 raw count; no hate crime law; social acceptance rising (72% accepting 2022); political backing for decriminalisation; pride parades held peacefully. So: criminalisation on books (secondary for trans), documented police extortion as lever (rule 2 — documented lever used), justice system failure against a trans person (magistrate refusal, case dismissed), documented pattern of violence against trans women (69 over 5 years), no recourse machinery. Society relatively tolerant and improving. Mix: tier 2/3 — state-tolerated targeting (police extortion) with thin recourse, plus documented violence pattern with institutional failure. That's around 0.42-0.50. Cross-dressing law struck down is a positive. Police extortion documented as pattern by equality org director. I'd say 0.47.

Hmm, compare 3 vs 5. Dossier 5 has documented police extortion lever, documented violence pattern (69 cases), documented state failure (court refusal). Dossier 3 has no documented trans-specific incidents at all, but strong societal hostility and no recourse. Dossier 3's negatives are mostly resident-facing (marriage, AD law) plus social attitudes. Rule 13: documented societal hostility with thin recourse = tier 3. Dossier 5 has tier 2 (state-tolerated targeting — police extortion) documented. So 5 should be below 3? Police extortion of LGBT people documented is state-tolerated targeting. But society in 5 is more accepting (72%). Dossier 5: extortion is mostly against "men in compromising positions" and sex workers; the trans-specific record is violence + justice failure. Hmm.

Rule 14 precedence: dossier 5's worst feature = tier 2/3 mix (police extortion using sodomy law as lever, documented; justice-system failure against trans woman; violence pattern). Dossier 3's worst = tier 3 societal hostility with no documented trans-specific targeting. Also 3 has no documented border/facility exposure either.

I think 5 slightly below 3? Or 3 below 5? Let's consider: In dossier 5, a trans visitor outed faces: possible police extortion using residual laws, violence with weak recourse (magistrate dismissed case). In dossier 3, outed visitor faces: social disapproval, possible service refusal, no legal protections, but no documented targeting. Rule 2 says where the statute's lever is documented (dossier 5: police using summary jurisdiction to extort LGBT), it weighs. Rule 13 says a latent tangential statute plus open questions plus thin recourse holds a step below acceptance-with-protections.

I'd put dossier 5 around 0.45 and dossier 3 around 0.50. Hmm but 5 has documented violence pattern (69 cases, state called to act) and justice failure; 3 has none documented but a hostile religious climate. Also 3's LGR requires surgery — resident. Actually the "no documented targeting" in 3 is in a thin-data record? The dossier 3 record seems moderately well-documented (ILGA overview, rights index, news). Silence there = moderately positive signal in a well-documented state.

Let me settle: D3 = 0.52, D5 = 0.46.

Actually reconsider D5's acceptance: 72% accepting, decriminalisation supported by majority of parties, cross-dressing law struck down, pride without violence. Negatives: sodomy law with life penalty as police lever (documented extortion), no LGR, no hate crime, justice failure case (2017 — dated, 9 years ago), 69 violence cases 2018-2022 (raw count). The violence count without denominator — but it's a documented pattern prompting regional commission action, state implicated by failure to act. Dossier 5 is likely a small country (raw counts matter more in small jurisdictions). Score ~0.45-0.48.

Dossier 1: let me reconsider. Article 521 directly criminalises trans feminine presentation with up to 6 years. Court practice: Article 534 declining application but still arrests, anal examinations, 2012 cinema raid (36 arrested). Police arresting LGBT people. Documented rise in prejudice and violence in capital. Government restricted LGBT gatherings (frozen by court). Active hostile climate plus a direct criminal statute against trans expression with documented enforcement. That's clearly in high-risk/severe band. Rule: state-imposed criminalisation of trans expression = tier above. Compare calibration 0.25-A (raids detaining people for appearance inconsistency, extortions) = 0.25. Dossier 1 has an explicit statute criminalising trans feminine presentation, prosecuted. Enforcement evidence is somewhat dated (2012 raid, 2018 arrest) plus 2022 rise in prejudice/violence. Also court pushback. I'd say ~0.22-0.26. Let's go 0.24.

Hmm, but is enforcement current? "Court practice has moved against Article 534 without removing it... arrests and prosecutions have been brought under it" — the assessment states enforcement has included police arrests and anal examinations. The regional review says the state applies both de facto and explicit criminalisation of transgender expression. That's current-ish (country review). So explicit criminalisation current → strong. 0.20-0.24. I'll say 0.22.

Dossier 4 vs 2: D4 has more comprehensive machinery (X markers, custody preference protocol, criminalised transphobia, free surgery) but also documented significant violence/discrimination in practice (2026) and divergent prison practice in one state (residents). D2 has hate crime rising, mass shooting, but liberal society. D4's violence: "continue to face significant violence and discrimination in practice" per March 2026 review. D4 also prison census showing trans women in male units — resident sphere. Traveller-facing: no restrictions; positive protections. I'd rate D4 0.86, D2 0.79.

Actually D2's negatives: 8% reporting, falling clearance rate, 2022 mass shooting (30-year sentence = strong state response), record reports. Plus organized anti-trans movement (feminist networks) — social hostility framing trans as threat. But overall liberal, protections in force. ~0.78.

D4: protections strong and operating (court damages, custody protocol national, X markers). Violence significant but not organized targeting; dating-app robbery fatal in largest city (mentioned in source evidence: "robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal") — that's an axis E pattern affecting travelers using apps. Hmm, that's a real trans/LGB-adjacent risk for visitors. Also drink-spiking robberies targeting LGBTQIA+ people in major city during Pride — traveler-relevant. So D4 has some documented street risk alongside strong protections. 0.84-0.86. I'll give 0.85.

Final: 1: 0.22, 2: 0.79, 3: 0.52, 4: 0.85, 5: 0.46.

Reconsider 3 once more: no trans-specific criminal offence, no documented targeting, documented acceptance in one territory, but strong societal/religious hostility, no AD law, no hate-crime recognition, no LGR beyond surgery (resident). Rule 13: absence of resident machinery is lightest. Known traveler-facing exposure: none documented. Open questions: border, facilities. Social hostility: majority opposition to same-sex marriage, dominant religious institution opposing — that's moral-offender framing toward LGB; for trans visitors, is there documented hostility? The dossier doesn't document anti-trans violence or service refusal. But conservative climate with 12% approval. I'd say 0.52-0.55. Let's give 0.53.

And 5 at 0.46 — documented police extortion lever + justice failure + violence pattern vs. 3's absence of documented harm. Yes, 5 below 3.
